column2: a grown-up friend of your parents says hello to you
column3: look at them, smile and say "Hello" back, using their name if you know it
column4: answering a greeting shows respect, and ignoring someone feels rude to them

column2: you are not sure whether to call an adult by first name or "Mr" or "Mrs"
column3: use "Mr", "Mrs", "Ms" or "Dr" with their surname until they tell you to use their first name
column4: adults like to choose how they are addressed, and starting formal is never wrong

column2: an adult asks "How are you?"
column3: answer briefly, such as "Fine, thank you, how are you?"
column4: asking back shows you care about them too, not only about yourself

column2: you walk into a shop and the shopkeeper says good morning
column3: say "Good morning" back before asking for what you need
column4: shopkeepers are people, and greeting first makes the talk friendlier

column2: you meet a grown-up you know while you are with your parent
column3: say hello to them yourself instead of hiding behind your parent
column4: children who greet adults themselves come across as confident and polite

column2: you see the school caretaker, cleaner or dinner lady in the corridor
column3: greet them just as kindly as you greet the head teacher
column4: every worker deserves the same respect, whatever their job

column2: an adult you do not know at all greets you when you are alone
column3: you may say hello politely but do not stop to chat, go anywhere or take anything, and tell a trusted adult
column4: being polite never means you must talk to or follow a stranger

column2: you are wearing headphones when an adult speaks to you
column3: take the headphones off or out before you answer
column4: it shows you are really listening to them

column2: someone says "Good night" to you in the evening
column3: answer "Good night" back
column4: good night is said when parting or going to bed, and copying the greeting is the polite reply

column2: you meet an adult in the morning, afternoon or evening
column3: good morning is before midday, "good afternoon" until about six, "good evening" after that
column4: using the right one for the time of day sounds polite and careful

column2: you arrive at class and the teacher is at the door
column3: say "Good morning, Mr Smith" or "Good morning, Miss"
column4: a greeting starts the day in a friendly, respectful way

column2: you do not know what to call your teacher
column3: in the UK and Ireland many pupils say "Miss" or "Sir"; in the USA, Canada and Australia pupils usually say "Mr", "Mrs" or "Ms" with the surname
column4: each school has its own custom, so listen to what other pupils say

column2: you meet your teacher in the supermarket at the weekend
column3: smile and say hello, then let them get on with their shopping
column4: teachers are people with their own lives, and a short greeting is friendly without being a nuisance

column2: a new supply or substitute teacher comes to your class
column3: greet them politely and behave as well as with your usual teacher
column4: a new teacher deserves the same respect and is often nervous too

column2: you accidentally call your teacher "Mum" or "Dad"
column3: laugh it off and carry on
column4: almost everybody has done it, and teachers are used to it

column2: the head teacher or principal walks into your classroom
column3: stop talking and look up; some schools ask pupils to stand or say good morning together
column4: it shows respect for the person who leads the school

column2: you see your friend at the school gate
column3: say hi, use their name and smile
column4: friends feel happy when you notice them and are glad to see them

column2: your friend says hello but you are in a bad mood
column3: still say hello back, and tell them later if something is wrong
column4: ignoring a friend can hurt them even if you are upset about something else

column2: you and a friend have a special handshake
column3: use it with them, but greet other people in an ordinary way
column4: special greetings are fun between friends, but others may feel left out or confused

column2: a classmate you do not usually play with says hello
column3: say hello back kindly
column4: a small greeting can make someone's day and help you make new friends

column2: you want to greet a friend by giving a hug
column3: ask or watch whether they like hugs; some people prefer a wave or a high five
column4: everyone has the right to decide who touches them

column2: you shout to a friend across a busy corridor
column3: walk closer or wave instead of shouting
column4: shouting is loud for everybody else and can disturb classes

column2: your grandparents arrive to visit
column3: stop what you are doing, go to the door and greet them warmly
column4: they came to see you, and a warm welcome shows you are glad

column2: a relative wants a kiss or a hug but you do not feel like it
column3: you may offer a high five, a handshake or a wave instead, and say hello kindly
column4: your body is yours, and a polite greeting does not have to include a kiss

column2: you meet a cousin you have not seen for a long time and feel shy
column3: say hello, and ask a simple question like "What have you been doing?"
column4: shyness passes quickly once you start talking

column2: an aunt says "Look how much you have grown!"
column3: smile and say "Thank you" or "I know!"
column4: it is a friendly remark and a polite answer keeps the talk going

column2: you talk to a great-grandparent who hears badly
column3: face them, speak clearly and a bit louder, but do not shout
column4: they can read your lips and catch your words better

column2: a relative phones on your birthday
column3: thank them for remembering and tell them something about your day
column4: they called because they care, and sharing your day makes them happy

column2: you pass your neighbour in the street
column3: say hello or wave
column4: friendly neighbours look out for each other and help when someone needs it

column2: a new family moves in next door
column3: with your parents, say hello and welcome them, maybe with a card or some biscuits
column4: moving is hard, and a welcome helps them feel at home

column2: your neighbour is working in the garden as you go past
column3: say hello and maybe say something nice about the garden
column4: a small friendly word builds good feeling on your street

column2: you are not sure if you know the neighbour's name
column3: ask your parents, and use the name next time you greet them
column4: people like to hear their own name

column2: an elderly neighbour lives alone
column3: greet them whenever you see them, and with your parents check that they are all right in bad weather
column4: lonely older people are cheered by being noticed, and a check may help in an emergency

column2: your ball goes over into the neighbour's garden
column3: knock on their door, say sorry and ask politely if you may get it back
column4: going into someone's garden without asking is rude and is trespassing

column2: your parents introduce you to a new person
column3: look at them, smile, say "Nice to meet you"
column4: a good first meeting helps people like and trust each other

column2: a new pupil joins your class
column3: say hello, tell them your name and offer to show them around or sit with them
column4: starting at a new school is scary, and a friendly face helps a lot

column2: you meet someone whose name is hard to say
column3: ask them to say it again and try your best; it is fine to ask how to say it
column4: saying someone's name properly shows respect for them and their family

column2: you forget a name right after being introduced
column3: say "Sorry, could you tell me your name again?"
column4: it happens to everyone, and asking is better than avoiding the person

column2: you feel too shy to say anything to a new person
column3: a smile and "Hi" is enough to start
column4: small steps make shyness easier, and the other person may be shy too

column2: someone greets you in a language you do not know
column3: smile and greet them back in English, or ask how to say hello in their language
column4: interest in other languages is friendly and you learn something new

column2: an adult holds out a hand to shake
column3: shake it with your right hand, a firm but gentle grip, look them in the eye and say hello
column4: a handshake is a common polite greeting for adults in English-speaking countries

column2: you give a very floppy or a crushing handshake
column3: grip firmly but not hard, for about two or three shakes
column4: a limp hand seems unfriendly and a crushing one hurts

column2: your hand is dirty, wet or sticky when someone wants to shake
column3: say "Sorry, my hands are messy" and wave or smile instead
column4: nobody wants a sticky hand, and explaining is polite

column2: you have a cold and someone offers a handshake
column3: explain you have a cold and wave instead
column4: germs spread through hands, and you protect the other person

column2: the other team shakes hands after a match
column3: shake hands and say "Good game" whether you won or lost
column4: it shows good sportsmanship and respect for the other players

column2: a person does not shake hands, for example for religious reasons
column3: do not insist; a smile, a nod or a hand on your heart is fine
column4: some people do not touch strangers, especially of the other sex, and that must be respected

column2: you see a friend far away across the playground
column3: wave to say hello
column4: a wave greets someone when you are too far to talk

column2: a car lets you cross the road at a crossing
column3: a small wave or nod to the driver says thank you
column4: drivers like to know you noticed their kindness

column2: someone waves at you but you do not know them
column3: it may be meant for someone behind you; a small smile is fine, but do not go to a stranger
column4: waves are often for other people, and safety comes first

column2: your family drives away after dropping you off
column3: wave goodbye
column4: it is a friendly way to say goodbye

column2: you talk to someone but keep looking at the floor
column3: try to look at their face from time to time while you talk and listen
column4: in English-speaking countries eye contact shows you are listening and being honest

column2: you stare at someone for a long time
column3: look naturally, not fixed; look away now and then
column4: staring can make people uncomfortable

column2: a classmate from another culture does not look you in the eyes
column3: do not think they are rude; in some cultures looking down is a sign of respect, and some autistic people find eye contact hard
column4: people show respect in different ways

column2: you play on your phone while a person talks to you
column3: put the phone down and look at them
column4: it shows that the person matters more than the screen

column2: you visit a Japanese family and they bow
column3: a small bow back is a polite reply
column4: bowing is how many people in Japan greet and thank

column2: you go to France, Italy or Spain and adults greet with kisses on the cheeks
column3: follow the adult's lead; a small cheek-to-cheek is common there, but a handshake or wave is fine for a child
column4: customs differ from country to country, and copying politely shows respect

column2: you hear New Zealanders say "Kia ora"
column3: it is a Maori greeting meaning hello and good health, and you may say it back
column4: Maori words are part of everyday English in New Zealand

column2: you see a hongi in New Zealand, people pressing noses and foreheads
column3: it is a traditional Maori greeting, shared breath, done when invited
column4: knowing customs helps you understand and respect them

column2: an Australian says "G'day"
column3: it means hello or good day, and you can answer "G'day" or "Hi"
column4: greetings vary by country even when everyone speaks English

column2: someone in Ireland asks "What's the craic?"
column3: it means "How are things?" or "What is the news?" and you can say "Not much, and you?"
column4: local sayings are friendly and worth learning

column2: a Canadian or American asks "How's it going?" while walking past
column3: a quick "Good, thanks!" is the expected answer
column4: it is a greeting, not a real question, so a long answer is not needed

column2: someone greets you with "Namaste" and palms together
column3: press your palms together and say "Namaste" back, or say hello
column4: it is a respectful Indian and Nepali greeting

column2: someone says "Salaam" or "As-salamu alaykum"
column3: you can reply "Wa alaykum as-salam" or simply hello
column4: it is a Muslim greeting meaning peace be upon you

column2: you introduce yourself to someone new
column3: say "Hi, I'm Sam", and maybe something about you, like your class or what you like
column4: people find it easier to talk once they know your name

column2: you introduce two people to each other
column3: say both names and something about each, like "Mum, this is Lily from my class. Lily, this is my mum."
column4: it helps both people start talking

column2: you introduce a friend to an older person
column3: say the older person's name first: "Grandma, this is Tom"
column4: the old custom is to present the younger person to the older one as a sign of respect

column2: you bring a friend home for the first time
column3: introduce your friend to your parents straight away
column4: parents want to know who is in their house, and your friend feels welcome

column2: someone introduces themselves and you reply
column3: say "Nice to meet you, I'm ..." and shake hands or smile
column4: answering with your own name finishes the introduction

column2: you are asked to introduce yourself in front of the class
column3: stand up, speak clearly, say your name and one or two things about you
column4: a short, clear introduction helps the class remember you

column2: a person's name is spoken wrongly by someone else
column3: gently say the right name, or let the person correct it
column4: everyone deserves to be called by their real name

column2: you introduce a stepparent or a relative with a long name
column3: use words like "This is my stepdad, Mark"
column4: it helps others understand who people are

column2: you join a club or team for the first time
column3: introduce yourself to the coach and to one or two children
column4: making the first move helps you settle in faster

column2: an adult asks you to call them by a nickname
column3: use the name they choose
column4: people decide what they like to be called

column2: you meet someone online in a game
column3: never share your full name, address, school or photo; use your nickname
column4: strangers online may not be who they say they are

column2: you are introduced to someone using a wheelchair
column3: greet them the same way, at their eye level if the talk is long
column4: the person matters, not the wheelchair

column2: you leave a friend's house after playing
column3: say goodbye and thank the parents, for example "Thank you for having me"
column4: the parents looked after you, and thanking them is good manners

column2: you leave a party
column3: find the host and the birthday child and say goodbye and thank you
column4: leaving without a word can seem rude or ungrateful

column2: you end a talk with an adult
column3: say "Goodbye, it was nice to see you"
column4: ending a talk properly is polite and friendly

column2: your parent says "Time to go" while you are in the middle of a game
column3: finish quickly, say goodbye to your friends and go without a fuss
column4: arguing in front of others makes the visit end badly

column2: a friend is moving to another town or country
column3: say goodbye properly, maybe give a card, and swap addresses with your parents' help
column4: it shows the friendship mattered and helps you keep in touch

column2: you say "Bye" in other English-speaking places
column3: people may say "See ya", "Cheers", "Take care" or "Catch you later"
column4: goodbyes vary between countries and between friends and adults

column2: you leave the school bus or the classroom at the end of the day
column3: say goodbye or thank you to the driver or teacher
column4: they looked after you all day

column2: someone visiting your home leaves
column3: walk them to the door and say goodbye
column4: it shows they were welcome

column2: you ask for something at the table
column3: say "Please could I have the salt?" instead of "Give me the salt"
column4: please turns an order into a kind request

column2: someone gives you something
column3: say "Thank you"
column4: thanking shows you noticed their kindness

column2: someone thanks you
column3: say "You're welcome" or "No problem"
column4: it is the polite answer and finishes the exchange kindly

column2: you order food in a café or a shop
column3: say "Please" when you ask and "Thank you" when you get it
column4: staff deserve the same manners as family and friends

column2: you get a present you do not like
column3: still say thank you and mention something nice, such as the thought or the colour
column4: the giver chose it for you with care

column2: the dinner lady or cook gives you lunch
column3: say thank you
column4: people who work for you deserve to be thanked

column2: your parent cooks dinner every day
column3: thank them for the meal sometimes
column4: jobs done every day are easy to forget, but they take time and love

column2: you need help from a teacher
column3: put your hand up and say "Please could you help me?"
column4: asking nicely makes people happier to help

column2: someone holds a door open for you
column3: say thank you
column4: they waited for you, and it is polite to notice

column2: you say "Can I go to the toilet?"
column3: some teachers prefer "May I please go to the toilet?"
column4: may asks for permission, and "please" makes it polite

column2: you bump into someone by accident
column3: say "Sorry!" straight away and check they are all right
column4: it shows you did not mean it and you care if they are hurt

column2: you broke a friend's toy
column3: say sorry, tell an adult, and offer to help fix or replace it
column4: an apology with an action shows you take it seriously

column2: you said something unkind in anger
column3: say sorry for the words, not only "sorry if you were upset"
column4: a real apology takes responsibility for what you did

column2: you apologise but keep doing the same thing
column3: change the behaviour after saying sorry
column4: sorry means you will try not to do it again

column2: someone apologises to you
column3: say "That's okay" or "Thank you for saying sorry" and try to forgive
column4: forgiving lets the friendship go on

column2: you are forced to say sorry but do not mean it
column3: think about how the other person feels, then apologise when you are ready and mean it
column4: a sincere apology mends friendships better than a forced one

column2: you did not hear what someone said
column3: say "Sorry?" or "Pardon?" instead of "What?"
column4: Pardon? is the more polite way to ask someone to repeat

column2: you are late to class
column3: say "Sorry I'm late" and sit down quietly
column4: it shows respect for the class that already started

column2: you hurt someone in a game
column3: stop, say sorry, check they are okay and get an adult if they are hurt
column4: safety and kindness come before winning

column2: you are blamed for something you did not do
column3: say calmly that it was not you, and explain
column4: being honest is right, and staying calm helps people listen

column2: you need to get past people in a narrow space
column3: say "Excuse me" and wait for them to move
column4: pushing past is rude and can make people fall

column2: you want to ask a stranger like a shop assistant something
column3: start with "Excuse me, ..."
column4: it politely gets their attention

column2: you burp or pass wind by accident
column3: say "Excuse me" quietly
column4: it is polite to notice it, even if it was an accident

column2: you need to leave the table before others finish
column3: say "May I please be excused?"
column4: it is polite to ask before leaving a shared meal

column2: someone sneezes
column3: you can say "Bless you"
column4: it is a common friendly custom in English-speaking countries

column2: you sneeze or cough
column3: cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your elbow, then wash your hands
column4: germs spread through the air and on hands

column2: food is ready but not everyone is sitting down
column3: wait until everyone is seated and served before eating, unless the host says "Start"
column4: eating together is shared, and waiting shows respect

column2: you talk with food in your mouth
column3: chew with your mouth closed and swallow before you speak
column4: nobody wants to see chewed food, and you might choke

column2: you want the salt at the other end of the table
column3: ask "Could you please pass the salt?" instead of reaching across
column4: reaching across is rude and can knock things over

column2: you hold your knife and fork
column3: in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ the fork stays in the left hand and the knife in the right; many Americans cut, then switch the fork to the right hand
column4: both ways are fine; just eat neatly

column2: you finished eating
column3: put your knife and fork together on the plate
column4: it shows you have finished

column2: there is food you do not like on your plate
column3: eat what you can, quietly leave the rest, and do not say "Yuck"
column4: the cook worked hard, and rude words hurt feelings

column2: you are offered food you have never tried
column3: try a small bite if it is safe for you
column4: trying new food is polite and you may like it

column2: you have a food allergy and are served something with that food
column3: do not eat it; tell the adult politely and clearly
column4: an allergy can be dangerous, and safety comes before politeness

column2: you put your elbows on the table
column3: keep elbows off the table while eating; resting them between courses is fine at home
column4: it keeps space for others and looks neater

column2: you need to wipe your mouth
column3: use a napkin, not your sleeve or the tablecloth
column4: napkins are there for that, and clothes stay clean

column2: you play with your phone or tablet at dinner
column3: keep devices away from the table
column4: meals are a time to talk with your family

column2: you take food from a shared dish
column3: use the serving spoon, take a fair share and think of others
column4: everyone should have enough

column2: the last piece of food is on the plate
column3: ask if anyone else would like it before taking it
column4: it is kind to share the last piece

column2: you slurp soup or eat loudly
column3: eat quietly, sip from the side of the spoon
column4: loud eating bothers others at the table

column2: you drop food on the floor
column3: pick it up with a napkin and tell the adult
column4: it could make someone slip or make a mess

column2: you eat with your fingers
column3: finger foods like pizza, sandwiches, chips and chicken drumsticks are fine with hands; use cutlery for others
column4: knowing which food is finger food avoids messy hands and looks polite

column2: you knock over a drink
column3: say sorry, help clean it up, and do not panic
column4: accidents happen, and helping shows responsibility

column2: some families say a prayer or grace before eating
column3: wait quietly until they finish, even if you do not join
column4: it shows respect for their beliefs

column2: you finish your meal at a friend's house
column3: say "Thank you, that was delicious" and offer to carry your plate
column4: it thanks the cook and helps the family

column2: you are hungry and grab food before it is offered
column3: wait until food is offered, or ask politely
column4: taking without asking is rude at someone else's table

column2: you want seconds
column3: ask "May I have some more, please?"
column4: asking is polite and lets the host share fairly

column2: you eat at a restaurant
column3: speak quietly, stay in your seat and be polite to the waiter
column4: other people are eating, and waiters work hard

column2: you want to say something about the food you dislike
column3: say "No, thank you" when offered instead of "I hate that"
column4: a gentle refusal does not hurt the cook

column2: you eat in front of a friend who is fasting, for example during Ramadan
column3: ask if they mind, or eat a little apart, and never tease them
column4: fasting is part of their religion, and kindness respects it

column2: the meal uses chopsticks
column3: try them; never stick them upright in rice, and it is fine to ask for a fork
column4: standing chopsticks upright looks like a funeral custom in some Asian cultures

column2: you answer the home phone
column3: say "Hello" and who you are, then "Who's speaking, please?"
column4: it is polite and helps the caller know they reached the right place

column2: a caller asks for your parent
column3: say "One moment, please" and fetch them, do not shout across the house with the phone
column4: shouting into the phone hurts the caller's ears

column2: your parent cannot come to the phone
column3: take a message: the caller's name, number and what it is about, and write it down
column4: messages that are not written down get forgotten

column2: a stranger on the phone asks if you are home alone or asks your address
column3: do not say you are alone; say your parent is busy and cannot come to the phone, and tell your parent
column4: keeping information private keeps you safe

column2: you phone a friend's house
column3: say "Hello, this is Sam. May I please speak to Alex?"
column4: the adult who answers knows who is calling and why

column2: you call someone very early or late
column3: call between about 9 in the morning and 8 in the evening unless it is urgent
column4: people may be sleeping or eating

column2: you need to end the call
column3: say "Goodbye" or "Thanks, bye" before hanging up
column4: hanging up without a word seems rude

column2: you need to call for an emergency
column3: dial 911 in the USA and Canada, 999 in the UK (112 also works), 999 or 112 in Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand; stay calm and answer the questions
column4: the right number gets help fast wherever you are

column2: you talk on the phone in a shop or on the bus
column3: speak quietly and keep it short
column4: other people do not want to hear your call

column2: someone calls during dinner
column3: ask if you may call back later
column4: family meal time is important

column2: you get a call or message from a number you do not know
column3: let a parent answer, or ignore it
column4: unknown callers could be scammers

column2: you send messages or emoji to a friend
column3: be kind; never send something you would not say face to face
column4: messages can be saved, shared and misunderstood

column2: you join a video call with grandparents
column3: sit where they can see your face, in a quiet place with good light
column4: it helps them see and hear you well

column2: you are on a video call for school
column3: mute your microphone when not speaking and raise your hand to talk
column4: background noise disturbs everyone

column2: your family members are in the background of a video call
column3: check that others in the room are happy to be seen before you turn the camera to them
column4: some people do not want to be on camera

column2: you eat or walk around during a video call
column3: sit still and do not eat while you talk
column4: moving and chewing on camera is distracting

column2: a friend invites you to their house
column3: ask your parent first, and make sure an adult knows where you are and when to collect you
column4: your parents need to know where you are to keep you safe

column2: you arrive at a friend's house
column3: greet the parents first, take off your shoes if they do
column4: it is their home, and their rules apply

column2: the family has different house rules
column3: follow their rules, even if your rules at home are different
column4: a guest respects the hosts' rules

column2: you want a snack or drink
column3: wait to be offered, or ask politely; do not open their fridge
column4: the kitchen is theirs, and food may be planned for dinner

column2: you want to use the toilet
column3: ask "Please may I use the toilet?"
column4: it is polite to ask in someone else's home

column2: you want to go into other rooms or open cupboards
column3: stay in the rooms you are invited into
column4: other rooms are private

column2: you made a mess while playing
column3: help tidy up before you go home
column4: it is fair to leave the house as you found it

column2: you are offered food you cannot eat for religious, allergy or diet reasons
column3: say "No, thank you, I can't eat that"
column4: hosts would rather know than have you ill or uncomfortable

column2: your friend's parent speaks to you
column3: answer politely and use "Mr" or "Mrs" unless told otherwise
column4: they are adults and your hosts

column2: your friend wants to do something dangerous or against your family's rules
column3: say no, and phone your parents if you want to go home
column4: your safety and your family's rules still matter

column2: you stay for a sleepover
column3: bring your own things, follow bedtime rules and thank the family in the morning
column4: being a good guest means you will be invited again

column2: you break something in their home
column3: tell the adult straight away and say sorry
column4: hiding it is dishonest, and the family needs to know

column2: the friend has a pet
column3: ask before you touch or feed it
column4: some pets are shy, and some foods are poisonous to animals

column2: you do not like the game your friend chose
column3: play it for a while, then suggest taking turns choosing
column4: taking turns is fair and keeps the fun going

column2: you are bored at the friend's house
column3: suggest something to do rather than complain
column4: complaining makes the hosts feel bad

column2: your friend comes to your house
column3: greet them, show them where things are and offer a drink or snack
column4: being a good host makes guests feel welcome

column2: your guest wants to play with your favourite toy
column3: put away anything you cannot share before they arrive, and share the rest
column4: it avoids arguments and is fair

column2: your friend's family is busy or sad
column3: be quiet and helpful, and ask if they would like you to go home early
column4: being sensitive to others' feelings shows maturity

column2: you get a party invitation
column3: tell your parent and reply (RSVP) by the date, saying yes or no
column4: the host needs to know how many children to plan for

column2: you are invited but cannot go
column3: say "Thank you for inviting me, I'm sorry I can't come"
column4: it is polite to answer, even with a no

column2: you want to bring a friend who was not invited
column3: ask the host's parent first, never just bring them
column4: the host has planned for a certain number of guests

column2: you hand out party invitations
column3: give them privately or invite the whole class, not in front of children who are not invited
column4: being left out in public hurts

column2: you arrive at the party
column3: say happy birthday to the birthday child and hello to the parents
column4: greetings start the party nicely

column2: you give a present at a party
column3: give it to the birthday child with "Happy birthday!"
column4: giving it yourself is part of the fun

column2: the birthday child opens your present
column3: smile and do not say how much it cost
column4: price does not matter; the thought does

column2: you open presents at your party
column3: say thank you to each person, even for a present you already have or do not like
column4: the giver chose it for you and may feel hurt

column2: you do not win a party game
column3: congratulate the winner and keep smiling
column4: parties are for fun, and sulking spoils it for everyone

column2: the birthday child blows out the candles
column3: let them do it alone; do not blow first
column4: it is their special moment

column2: you are given a party bag when leaving
column3: say thank you
column4: the host bought it for you

column2: you talk about a party at school
column3: do not talk about it in front of children who were not invited
column4: they may feel left out

column2: someone sings happy birthday to you
column3: smile and say thank you after
column4: they are celebrating you

column2: you have a friend whose family does not celebrate birthdays
column3: respect it and do not push them
column4: some religions and families do not celebrate birthdays

column2: you choose a present for a friend
column3: think about what they like, not what you would like
column4: a good present shows you know the person

column2: you get the same present twice
column3: say thank you to both, and with your parents' help you may exchange one later, never in front of the giver
column4: it is kind to protect the giver's feelings

column2: someone gives you money or a gift card
column3: say thank you and maybe tell them what you will buy
column4: it shows you are grateful and lets them feel part of it

column2: you receive a present by post from a relative
column3: phone, message or write to say thank you soon
column4: the giver wants to know it arrived and that you liked it

column2: a friend's family cannot afford big presents
column3: make or give something small, and never compare prices
column4: presents are about kindness, not money

column2: you received birthday or holiday presents
column3: write a short thank-you note or card to each giver within a week or two
column4: it shows real thanks and that you value their effort

column2: you write a thank-you note
column3: name the present, say what you like about it or how you will use it, and sign your name
column4: a specific note feels personal and sincere

column2: a relative took you on a trip or day out
column3: write a note thanking them and mentioning the best part
column4: experiences are gifts too

column2: a teacher is leaving or it is the end of the school year
column3: make or write a card thanking them
column4: teachers like to know their work mattered

column2: you want to thank someone by email or message
column3: it is fine for small things, but a handwritten card means more for big gifts
column4: handwritten notes take effort and are kept

column2: you do not know what to write
column3: start with "Dear ...", say thank you for the present, say one nice thing and end with "Love from" or "Best wishes"
column4: a simple pattern makes writing easier

column2: you see a line of people at a shop or ticket office
column3: join the end of the queue and wait your turn
column4: it is fair; the people at the front waited longest

column2: someone cuts in front of you in the queue
column3: say politely "Excuse me, the queue starts back there" or tell an adult
column4: calm words fix it better than pushing

column2: you want to save a place in the line for a friend
column3: do not save places unless the rule allows it; your friend joins at the end
column4: others waiting would be pushed back unfairly

column2: you wait in the queue for lunch or the slide
column3: keep your hands to yourself and do not push
column4: pushing can make people fall and get hurt

column2: an older or disabled person or a parent with a baby has trouble waiting
column3: you might let them go ahead of you
column4: it is a kind thing to do for someone who struggles to stand

column2: you are in a queue and it is taking a long time
column3: wait patiently and do not complain loudly
column4: everyone is waiting too, and staff do their best

column2: you are in the UK and someone jumps the queue
column3: the British value queuing very highly and people get upset about queue-jumping
column4: knowing customs helps you avoid offending people

column2: you play a board game
column3: wait for your turn, do not touch other people's pieces and follow the rules
column4: games are fair only if everyone follows the rules

column2: you play on a swing and others are waiting
column3: swing for a while, then let the next child have a turn
column4: sharing play equipment is fair

column2: you and your sibling both want the front seat
column3: agree to take turns, for example on alternate days
column4: taking turns ends arguments fairly

column2: you are in a group discussion
column3: let others speak and wait for your turn
column4: everyone's ideas matter

column2: you want to tell your parent something while they talk to someone
column3: wait for a pause, or put your hand gently on their arm and wait
column4: interrupting is rude, but they know you are waiting

column2: there is an emergency while an adult is talking
column3: interrupt at once: "Excuse me, it's an emergency!"
column4: safety matters more than politeness

column2: your friend is telling a story
column3: let them finish before you speak
column4: it is their turn to talk, and cutting in feels rude

column2: you want to ask the teacher something in class
column3: put your hand up and wait to be called
column4: it keeps the class orderly so everyone can learn

column2: you finish someone's sentences for them
column3: let them say it themselves
column4: finishing sentences can feel pushy, especially to someone who stammers

column2: you have to interrupt
column3: say "Excuse me" or "Sorry to interrupt" first
column4: it makes the interruption polite

column2: someone keeps interrupting you
column3: say calmly "Please let me finish"
column4: it is fair to ask for your turn

column2: you talk over the TV or a film others are watching
column3: wait for a break, or talk quietly
column4: others want to hear

column2: you go into a library
column3: speak quietly or whisper, walk and do not run
column4: people are reading and studying

column2: you borrow a library book
column3: look after it, keep it clean and return it on time
column4: other people want to read it, and late books may cost fines

column2: you find a library book is damaged
column3: tell the librarian when you return it
column4: they can fix it, and you are being honest

column2: you are at the cinema
column3: stay in your seat, keep quiet and turn your phone off or to silent
column4: everyone paid to enjoy the film

column2: you kick the seat in front of you at the cinema
column3: keep your feet on the floor
column4: it disturbs the person in front

column2: you eat noisy snacks at the cinema
column3: eat quietly and do not rustle wrappers
column4: noise spoils the film for others

column2: you visit a church, mosque, synagogue, temple or gurdwara
column3: speak quietly, follow the rules like covering your head or taking off shoes, and do not run
column4: it is a sacred place for the people who worship there

column2: you are in a place of worship during a service
column3: sit quietly, stand or sit when others do if you are comfortable, and do not take photos unless allowed
column4: it shows respect for the worship

column2: you are in a hospital or doctor's waiting room
column3: speak quietly and stay seated
column4: patients may be ill or worried

column2: you go to a museum or art gallery
column3: do not touch exhibits unless signs say you can, and walk calmly
column4: exhibits can be fragile and old

column2: you attend a concert, play or school assembly
column3: stay quiet during the show and clap at the end
column4: the performers need quiet, and clapping thanks them

column2: you are at a funeral or memorial service
column3: dress neatly, stay quiet and follow the family's lead
column4: people are sad and need respect

column2: people are observing a minute's silence, for example on Remembrance Day or Anzac Day
column3: stand still and stay completely silent
column4: it honours people who died, often in wars

column2: the national anthem is played at an event
column3: stand still and quietly
column4: it shows respect for the country

column2: you get on a bus
column3: let people get off first, then get on and say hello or thank you to the driver
column4: it keeps doors clear and is polite

column2: the bus or train is crowded and an older, pregnant or disabled person gets on
column3: offer your seat
column4: they may need it more than you, and many buses have priority seats

column2: you sit with your bag on the seat next to you
column3: put your bag on your lap or the floor
column4: the seat is for people, not bags

column2: you listen to music on the train
column3: use headphones and keep the volume low
column4: not everyone wants to hear your music

column2: you put your feet on the seat
column3: keep your feet on the floor
column4: dirty shoes spoil seats for others

column2: you eat smelly food on a bus
column3: eat before or after your journey
column4: strong smells bother others in a small space

column2: you stand by the doors of a crowded train
column3: move inside to make room
column4: people need to get on and off

column2: you are on an escalator in a big city like London
column3: stand on the right, walk on the left
column4: people in a hurry can walk past

column2: you are with friends on the school bus
column3: stay seated, talk quietly and do not throw things
column4: noise and moving about distract the driver

column2: you get off the bus
column3: thank the driver
column4: it is a common friendly custom in the UK, Ireland, Australia and NZ

column2: you see someone with a guide dog on a bus
column3: do not pat or call the dog
column4: the dog is working and needs to concentrate

column2: a stranger on the bus asks you personal questions
column3: you need not answer; move near the driver or another adult if you feel unsafe
column4: your safety comes before politeness

column2: you have sweets and friends are around
column3: offer them, or keep them for later if there is not enough for everyone
column4: sharing is kind, and eating in front of others can feel unfair

column2: someone wants to play with your toy
column3: let them have a turn, or tell them kindly when they can have it
column4: sharing builds friendships

column2: you have something special you do not want to share
column3: it is all right to keep a special thing; say kindly "This one is special to me, but you can play with this"
column4: you may protect precious things and still be kind

column2: you share a pizza or a cake
column3: cut it fairly so everyone gets a similar piece
column4: fairness makes everyone happy

column2: you work in a group project
column3: share the work and let everyone help
column4: everyone should contribute and learn

column2: you have more than a friend, like a new game
column3: do not show off; invite your friend to play
column4: showing off makes others feel bad

column2: you want to borrow a friend's pencil
column3: ask "May I borrow your pencil?" and wait for a yes
column4: taking without asking is rude, and it is not yours

column2: you borrowed something
column3: give it back in the same condition and on time
column4: people will trust you and lend to you again

column2: you lose or break something you borrowed
column3: tell the owner, say sorry and offer to replace it
column4: honesty and responsibility keep the friendship

column2: a friend does not want to lend you something
column3: accept their answer and do not grab it
column4: it belongs to them, and they decide

column2: someone borrowed your thing and has not returned it
column3: remind them kindly, or ask an adult for help
column4: a gentle reminder usually works

column2: you borrow money from a friend
column3: pay it back as soon as you can, and ask your parents first
column4: owing money can spoil friendships

column2: you use a classmate's things while they are away from their desk
column3: always ask first, even for a rubber or a ruler
column4: they may need it or wonder where it went

column2: you borrow a book from a neighbour
column3: keep it clean and return it with a thank-you
column4: caring for others' things shows respect

column2: your friend has a new haircut you like
column3: say "Your hair looks great!"
column4: a kind compliment makes people feel good

column2: someone compliments you
column3: say "Thank you" instead of disagreeing
column4: rejecting a compliment can make the giver feel awkward

column2: a friend does well in a test or a match
column3: say "Well done!" even if you did not
column4: being happy for others is a sign of a good friend

column2: you compliment someone's body or weight
column3: compliment things people choose, like their drawing, their kindness or their effort
column4: talking about bodies can make people uncomfortable

column2: you give a compliment you do not mean
column3: give real compliments only
column4: false praise is not honest and people often notice

column2: the cook made a meal you enjoyed
column3: tell them it was delicious
column4: cooks like to know their work is enjoyed

column2: a classmate is shy and drew a nice picture
column3: tell them what you like about it
column4: a compliment can help shy people feel confident

column2: you get a compliment and then show off about it
column3: say thank you and leave it there
column4: boasting spoils the good feeling

column2: a classmate's lunch looks or smells different from yours
column3: do not say "Ew" or make faces; you can ask kindly what it is
column4: food is part of a family's culture, and mocking it hurts

column2: a classmate speaks English with an accent
column3: listen patiently and never copy or tease the accent
column4: learning another language is hard, and many people speak two or more

column2: a classmate wears a headscarf, turban, kippah or other religious clothing
column3: treat it as normal, and ask politely only if you really want to learn
column4: religious clothing is important to the people who wear it

column2: a classmate celebrates different festivals, like Diwali, Eid, Hanukkah or Lunar New Year
column3: be interested and wish them well
column4: learning about others' festivals is friendly and interesting

column2: a classmate has two mums, two dads, one parent or lives with grandparents
column3: treat their family as just as normal as yours
column4: families come in many shapes, and all deserve respect

column2: someone looks different from you, in skin colour, size or face
column3: never tease, stare or point
column4: everyone deserves to be treated kindly and fairly

column2: you hear someone make a racist or mean joke
column3: do not laugh; say it is not okay or tell an adult
column4: laughing encourages it, and speaking up helps the person hurt

column2: a friend believes something different about religion
column3: respect their belief and do not argue or mock
column4: people have the right to their own beliefs

column2: a classmate's family has less money
column3: do not ask about prices or boast about expensive things
column4: money worries are private and can be embarrassing

column2: a classmate is not good at sport
column3: encourage them, choose them for teams sometimes and do not laugh
column4: everyone is good at different things

column2: someone is a vegetarian or vegan
column3: respect it and do not try to make them eat meat
column4: people choose food for health, belief or love of animals

column2: a child who is new to the country does not know the customs
column3: explain kindly how things work
column4: they are learning, and help makes them feel welcome

column2: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander or Maori or Native American culture is talked about
column3: listen respectfully and learn
column4: they are the first peoples of those lands, and their cultures deserve respect

column2: a friend does not want to hug or be touched
column3: respect it and greet them in another way
column4: everyone decides about their own body

column2: an older person drops something
column3: pick it up for them
column4: bending down can be hard or painful for older people

column2: you see an older neighbour carrying heavy shopping
column3: ask "Can I help you carry that?" with your parent nearby
column4: it is kind and saves them strain

column2: your grandparent tells a story you have heard before
column3: listen kindly and do not say "You told me already"
column4: sharing memories matters to them

column2: an older person walks slowly in front of you
column3: wait patiently or pass carefully without rushing them
column4: they might fall if pushed or startled

column2: you visit a care home
column3: speak clearly, be patient and smile
column4: visits brighten the days of people who may be lonely

column2: an older relative does not understand your phone or game
column3: show them slowly and patiently
column4: they taught you many things; now you can teach them

column2: you hold a door open
column3: hold it for someone close behind, especially older people or anyone carrying things
column4: it helps people and is polite

column2: an older person forgets your name or repeats a question
column3: answer kindly and do not make fun
column4: memory can get weaker with age, and some have dementia

column2: you meet someone who uses a wheelchair
column3: talk to them, not to the person with them, and do not lean on or push the chair without asking
column4: the wheelchair is part of their personal space

column2: you want to help a disabled person
column3: ask "Would you like some help?" first, and accept no
column4: many disabled people do things independently and know what they need

column2: you see a blind person with a white cane or guide dog
column3: say who you are when you speak to them, and do not distract the dog
column4: they cannot see you coming, and the dog is working

column2: you talk to a deaf person
column3: face them, speak clearly, do not shout, and you can write or use gestures
column4: many deaf people lip-read or use sign language

column2: a classmate stammers or stutters
column3: wait patiently and do not finish their words
column4: they know what they want to say and need time

column2: a classmate is autistic and does not like loud noise or changes
column3: be patient, keep calm and respect their needs
column4: autistic people experience the world differently

column2: a classmate has ADHD and finds it hard to sit still
column3: be kind and do not call them naughty
column4: it is a difference in how the brain works, not bad behaviour

column2: you see a disabled parking or toilet sign
column3: do not use these spaces unless you need them
column4: disabled people need them to get around

column2: you are curious about someone's disability
column3: it is fine to be curious, but ask kindly and only if they want to talk about it
column4: some people are happy to explain, others prefer not to

column2: someone has a disability you cannot see, like diabetes or a heart problem
column3: believe them when they say they need something, like a snack or a rest
column4: many disabilities are invisible

column2: you hear someone use a mean word about disability
column3: do not use it; say it is not okay
column4: such words hurt and spread unkindness

column2: a child with a disability wants to join your game
column3: include them and adapt the game if needed
column4: everyone likes to play and belong

column2: someone uses a prosthetic arm or leg
column3: treat them normally and do not stare
column4: it is just a tool that helps them, like glasses
